question_48.question: RC made a tar of my project with Starfish. I copied it to netscratch and extracted it there, but instead of my ProjectX folder I got this weird nested tree of empty directories with ProjectX way down at the bottom. Is the archive corrupt?
question_48.reference_answer: The archive is fine. Starfish tars in place and captures the entire path inside the tar file, so extracting recreates that whole path underneath your output directory. Extracting a Starfish tar of /n/holylabs/jharvard_lab/ProjectX into /n/netscratch/jharvard/temp gives you /n/netscratch/jharvard/temp/n/holylabs/jharvard_lab/ProjectX. Move the ProjectX directory to where you actually want it, then remove the leftover empty n/holylabs/jharvard_lab tree. Use plain `rm` rather than `rm -rf`, so it errors out if other files remain or you typed the wrong path.
question_48.answer:
No, the archive is not corrupt. This is expected behavior when using tar archives created by Starfish.

When Starfish creates a tar archive, it captures the **entire absolute path** of the files inside the archive. So if you tarred `/n/holylabs/jharvard_lab/ProjectX`, the archive contains that full path. When you extract it anywhere, it recreates that full path relative to your extraction point.

For example, if you copy the tar to `/n/netscratch/jharvard/temp/` and run `tar -xf mystarfishtar.tar`, you'll end up with:
```
/n/netscratch/jharvard/temp/n/holylabs/jharvard_lab/ProjectX
```

**To avoid this**, you can extract the archive to a temporary location and then move just the `ProjectX` folder where you want it, or you can use the `--strip-components` option to remove the leading directories:

```bash
tar -xf mystarfishtar.tar --strip-components=4 -C /n/netscratch/jharvard/temp/
```

This strips the first 4 path components (`n/`, `holylabs/`, `jharvard_lab/`, and the parent directory), leaving just `ProjectX` at the extraction point.

See [Tips for using tar to archive data](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/tips-for-tar-archiving) for more details.

messages.tool_args: RC made a tar of my project with Starfish. I copied it to netscratch and extracted it there, but instead of my ProjectX folder I got this weird nested tree of empty directories with ProjectX way down at the bottom. Is the archive corrupt?

messages.content:
No, the archive is not corrupt. This is expected behavior when using tar archives created by Starfish.

When Starfish creates a tar archive, it captures the **entire absolute path** of the files inside the archive. So if you tarred `/n/holylabs/jharvard_lab/ProjectX`, the archive contains that full path. When you extract it anywhere, it recreates that full path relative to your extraction point.

For example, if you copy the tar to `/n/netscratch/jharvard/temp/` and run `tar -xf mystarfishtar.tar`, you'll end up with:
```
/n/netscratch/jharvard/temp/n/holylabs/jharvard_lab/ProjectX
```

**To avoid this**, you can extract the archive to a temporary location and then move just the `ProjectX` folder where you want it, or you can use the `--strip-components` option to remove the leading directories:

```bash
tar -xf mystarfishtar.tar --strip-components=4 -C /n/netscratch/jharvard/temp/
```

This strips the first 4 path components (`n/`, `holylabs/`, `jharvard_lab/`, and the parent directory), leaving just `ProjectX` at the extraction point.

question_49.question: I already pushed a bunch of archives into our lab's tape area on Globus and then realized I named them badly. Can I just rename them, or move a couple into a different folder to tidy things up?
question_49.reference_answer: No — do not delete, move, or rename data once it has been transferred to the tape buffer. The Globus buffer gives you write access to upload data destined for tape, and all changes within your lab's Globus collection are automatically picked up by the tape robot. Deletions on the Globus buffer may result in permanent deletion on tape, and deleting files that have already been placed on tape removes the 'link' and makes retrieval impossible. Mass deletions, moves, and file renaming require cumbersome manual intervention. Name files appropriately before you transfer them, and work with your PI or lab data manager on your lab's tape storage protocols.
question_49.answer:
Yes, you can rename and move files within the tape staging area using Globus.

Here's what you need to know:

*   **Rename & Move:** Since the tape staging area is a disk-based filesystem accessible via Globus, you can use the Globus File Manager to rename files and move them into different folders to organize them [Globus: Transfer Data to Tape](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/tape-globus-access/).
*   **Permissions:** Note that read/write access applies to the whole lab collection on Globus, and there is no way to restrict permissions on individual folders within the collection [Globus: Transfer Data to Tape](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/tape-globus-access/).
*   **Tape Migration:** Keep in mind that data in the staging area is eventually migrated to tape. Once data is on tape, it cannot be modified or renamed; it must be retrieved back to the staging area first if changes are needed.

If you run into any issues with the File Manager, you can also access the underlying filesystem via SSH/SCP to perform the renames/moves, though Globus is the primary interface for this storage.

question_50.question: Our PI wants to let a postdoc read and write only one project folder inside our lab's tape collection on Globus, not the rest of it. How do we set that up?
question_50.reference_answer: You cannot. There is no way to restrict permissions on individual folders within your lab tape collection — read/write access applies to the whole lab collection on Globus. The underlying filesystem is not owned by FASRC, so FASRC cannot set those permissions; everyone with access is essentially a guest on the NESE tape system. (The PI and General Manager can add lab members to the collection, but only to all of it.)
question_50.answer:
Globus on FASRC exposes only the **`Lab`** and **`Users/$USER`** directories — everything else (like `Everyone` or `Transfer`) is invisible through Globus [Globus File Transfer](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/globus-file-transfer/).

To let a postdoc read/write **only one project folder** inside your lab's Globus share, you have two options:

### Option 1: Restrict POSIX permissions (recommended)
Globus uses your FASRC account's POSIX permissions, so you can control access at the filesystem level:

1. **Change the folder's group ownership** to a group that includes only the PI and postdoc (or create a new group for this purpose).
2. **Set permissions** so that only the owner and group members can read/write, and "other" has no access:
   ```bash
   chmod 770 /path/to/project_folder
   chown PI_user:project_group /path/to/project_folder
   ```
3. **Add the postdoc to the group** (if not already):
   ```bash
   usermod -a -G project_group postdoc_user
   ```

This way, even though the postdoc can see the parent `Lab` directory in Globus, they won't be able to read or write the project folder unless they have explicit permissions.

### Option 2: Create a separate subdirectory structure
If you want the postdoc to only see that one folder in Globus, you could:
1. Create a new parent directory inside `Lab` that contains only this project folder.
2. Restrict access to that parent directory so only the PI and postdoc can access it.

### Important notes
- Globus will use your FASRC account's permissions the same way you would if accessing storage from a cluster node [Globus File Transfer](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/globus-file-transfer/).
- You need read access to transfer files out and write access to copy files in.
- Symlinks do not work in Globus.

For more details on POSIX permissions, see [Understanding file and group permissions](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/understanding-permissions/).

question_51.question: On Cannon I just do salloc to grab a shell on a compute node, but on FASSE it doesn't work. How am I supposed to get an interactive session there?
question_51.reference_answer: salloc is deliberately unavailable on FASSE — it is disabled for security reasons, and FASSE does not allow interactive jobs from the command line at all. For interactive work you use the FASSE Open OnDemand (OOD) / VDI virtual desktop at https://fasseood.rc.fas.harvard.edu, reachable in your browser while connected to the FASRC VPN on the @fasse realm (note @fasse, not the @fasrc realm you use for Cannon). OOD gives you pre-built apps and interactive command-line access in a desktop-like environment. SSH to fasselogin.rc.fas.harvard.edu remains available for batch work.
question_51.answer:
Based on the available documentation, I don't have specific details on FASSE's interactive session policies. However, I can share some general context and suggest next steps:

**What I found:**
- FASSE is a separate FASRC cluster from Cannon, with its own login infrastructure and potentially different policies [FASSE OOD](https://fasseood.rc.fas.harvard.edu/)
- The documentation mentions FASSE uses its own VPN realm (`@fasse`) and has a separate Open OnDemand instance [About Usernames](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/about-usernames/)

**Why `salloc` might not work on FASSE:**
FASSE may have different SLURM policies than Cannon — for example, it might:
- Require `srun` instead of `salloc` for interactive sessions
- Restrict interactive allocations on certain partitions
- Have different resource limits or queue configurations

**Recommended next steps:**
1. Check the [FASSE documentation](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/fasse/) for cluster-specific guidance
2. Try `srun --pty /bin/bash` as an alternative to `salloc` for an interactive shell
3. Contact FASRC support or check the [FASRC Quickstart Guide](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/quickstart-guide/) for cluster-specific instructions

question_53.reference_answer: 140.247.232.228. All traffic to the Internet from FASSE — VPN, login, compute, or fasseood — goes out through the FASRC proxy (rcproxy.rc.fas.harvard.edu), which currently has that external IP address. It is subject to change, so you can confirm it by running `curl icanhazip.com` from the node you will actually be working on.
question_53.answer:
All outbound Internet traffic from FASSE (including from compute nodes) goes through the Harvard proxy (`rcproxy.rc.fas.harvard.edu:3128`), so external services see the proxy's public IP address rather than the compute node's internal address [FASSE Proxy Settings](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/proxy-settings/).

The current external IP address is **140.247.232.228**. You can verify this from a compute node by running:

```bash
curl icanhazip.com
```

This will return the IP address that the Internet sees you coming from. Note that this address is subject to change, so if you're unsure, you can run the `curl` command on the node you plan to use to confirm the current IP.

question_54.question: Our data use agreement says the data has to be encrypted at rest. I was planning to stage the intermediate files for my FASSE jobs in netscratch since it's fast. Is that OK?
question_54.reference_answer: No. If you have a DUA that requires encryption at rest, you must not use scratch for any data the DUA applies to — neither local scratch nor FASRC's global scratch supports encryption at rest. Separately, DSL 3 / FASSE data should not be stored in your home directory either. You are responsible for knowing and complying with the applicable Harvard Information Security Policy, the Harvard Research Data Security Policy, and any applicable contracts / data use agreements; if you are unsure how this applies to your data, consult FASRC at security@rc.fas.harvard.edu or your School Security Officer.
question_54.answer:
Based on the available documentation, I can provide some guidance, but I need to be upfront about limitations:

**The documentation doesn't explicitly state whether netscratch provides encryption at rest.** Here's what I can tell you:

1. **netscratch is a VAST filesystem** — it's a high-performance scratch storage system on the FASRC clusters [FAQ](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/faq).

2. **Data Use Agreements require compliance** — Before any confidential, proprietary, or sensitive data is stored on FASRC, it must be properly classified and any DUA must be in place [Data and Data Use Agreements (DUA)](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/data-use-agreements/). The project PI is responsible for ensuring compliance.

3. **Data Security Levels (DSL)** — Harvard classifies data into 5 security levels, and the DSL determines how data must be managed [Data Security Levels](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/data-security-levels/).

**What you should do:**

Since the documentation doesn't explicitly confirm whether netscratch provides encryption at rest, you should:

1. **Contact FASRC support** to confirm whether netscratch volumes are encrypted at rest
2. **Consult your PI** — they are responsible for DUA compliance
3. **Check with Harvard Information Security** about whether netscratch meets your specific DUA requirements

If netscratch does *not* provide encryption at rest, you may need to:
- Use a different storage location that does provide encryption
- Encrypt the data yourself before staging it to netscratch
- Work with FASRC to identify a compliant storage solution

question_55.question: Our level 3 project storage doesn't show up as a collection in Globus at all. What do we have to do to get it added?
question_55.reference_answer: Nothing is broken: DSL 3 / FASSE storage is intentionally not included in Globus by default. To have it exposed, first review the governing DUA — Globus makes data available over the Internet without a VPN or private network, so a DUA requiring VPN/private-network access for all access to the data would not be Globus-compliant (consult your School Security Officer if unsure). Then submit a ticket to rchelp@rc.fas.harvard.edu that (1) includes the path to the project to add (e.g. /n/piname_project_l3), (2) states that the PI attests Globus is compliant with any contracts/DUAs governing the data, and (3) is either sent by the PI or receives a direct reply from the PI confirming it.
question_55.answer:
Based on the available documentation, I don't have specific information about "level 3 project storage" or why it might not appear as a Globus collection. 

However, here are some general things to check regarding Globus collections on FASRC:

1. **Globus is a third-party service** — Globus is not run by FASRC, but rather used as a file-sharing nexus [Globus File Transfer](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/globus-file-transfer/).

3. **Different storage types may have different access** — Some storage environments (like FASSE for protected data) have specific transfer requirements [FASSE / Protected Data Transfers](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/fasse-protected-data-transfers/).

Since "level 3 project storage" isn't covered in the available documentation, I'd recommend:

- Checking the [Globus File Transfer](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/globus-file-transfer/) guide for the specific setup steps
- Contacting FASRC support directly to ask about your specific storage environment and why it may not be appearing as a Globus collection

question_56.question: How much CPU and RAM am I actually allowed on the FASRC login server, and is there a cap on how many terminal windows I can have open at once?
question_56.reference_answer: Each login-node session is limited to 1 core and 8GB of memory, and you may have at most 5 sessions per user. Users who abuse the login nodes may have their sessions terminated, and the login nodes are rebooted during monthly maintenance to clear out stale sessions. If you need more than 5 sessions, switch to batch jobs, use Open OnDemand (which gives you a desktop with multiple terminals on a dedicated compute node), or use screen/tmux to multiplex one session.
question_56.answer:
Based on the available documentation, I cannot provide specific numeric limits for CPU, RAM, or terminal windows on the FASRC login servers. The indexed sources do not appear to cover these exact resource limits.

What the documentation does emphasize is that:

*   **Login nodes are for light use only** — The login servers (holylogin## and boslogin##) must be kept free of significant computation. You should not run jobs or heavy applications (like MATLAB or Mathematica) on them. They are a shared, multi-user resource, and you should use an interactive SLURM session or job for all applications and scripts beyond basic terminals, editors, etc. [Cluster Customs and Responsibilities](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/responsibilities)
*   **For graphical applications**, you should use [Open OnDemand](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/terminal-access) instead of the command line login. [Command line access with Terminal (login nodes)](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/terminal-access)

For specific resource limits (CPU, RAM, process counts, terminal sessions), you may need to:
1.  Check your current limits by running `ulimit -a` on a login node.
2.  Contact FASRC support directly for the official per-user resource caps on login nodes.

question_57.question: I ran ssh-copy-id and my key works great when I'm in the office, but from my apartment it still makes me punch in the 6-digit code every single time. Did the key not install properly?
question_57.reference_answer: The key is fine — this is by design. Passwordless (ssh-key) authentication is only permitted to the Cannon login nodes from Harvard networks, including Harvard/FASRC VPNs. If you connect from an external network you are still required to provide two-factor authentication regardless of your key. So either connect to the VPN from home, or accept the 2FA prompt. (On FASSE, passwordless ssh is permitted from the FASSE VPN only.) You can confirm the key installed by checking that it is present in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the cluster.
question_57.answer:
Based on the documentation, your SSH key is likely installed correctly, but the 6-digit code requirement is **expected behavior** and not a sign that the key failed to install.

Here's what's happening:

## SSH key authentication still requires 2FA

When you use SSH key authentication on FASRC login nodes, you bypass the **password** prompt, but you still need to provide the **6-digit OpenAuth token code** for two-factor authentication. This is documented in the [Command line access with Terminal (login nodes)](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/terminal-access/) guide, which states:

> "Once connected, enter the password you set after receiving your account confirmation email. When prompted for the Verification code, use the current 6-digit OpenAuth token code."

The key difference is:
- **In the office (Harvard network)**: You may be bypassing the 2FA prompt entirely due to network-based trust or cached credentials
- **From your apartment (outside Harvard network)**: The full authentication flow is enforced — SSH key authentication + 2FA OpenAuth code

## Your key is working fine

The fact that you're only prompted for the 6-digit code (and not a password) confirms that your SSH key **is** installed properly. If the key hadn't been installed correctly, you'd be prompted for your password instead.

## What you can do

1. **Continue entering the 6-digit code** — this is the expected behavior when connecting from outside the Harvard network
2. **Make sure your OpenAuth token app is ready** before connecting so you can quickly enter the current code
3. **Wait for the code to refresh** if you enter it incorrectly — the documentation warns that "Reusing the old code will result in error"

This is a security feature, not a configuration issue. The SSH key saves you from entering your password, but the 2FA requirement remains for connections from untrusted networks.

question_58.question: I'm an IQSS researcher and my survey data is classified Level 2. Which cluster am I supposed to be on, and what exactly goes in the VPN box versus the cluster login box?
question_58.reference_answer: Level 2 data belongs on Cannon, the FAS research computing cluster for Data Security Level 2 (only Level 3 data must move to the FASSE secure environment). To get on: in the Cisco AnyConnect VPN client use server address vpn.rc.fas.harvard.edu and enter your FASRC username in the format username@fasrc, your FASRC password, and your FASRC 2FA token — note this is NOT the code associated with your HarvardKey account. Then log into the Cannon cluster at https://rcood.rc.fas.harvard.edu using just your FASRC username WITHOUT the '@fasrc', plus your FASRC password.
question_58.answer:
Since your survey data is classified **Level 2**, you should be using the **Cannon** cluster. Cannon is the Faculty of Arts and Sciences research computing cluster specifically designated for users with Data Security Level 2 data. If your data were Level 3, you would need to use the FASSE cluster instead. [IQSS Cannon Quickstart Guide](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/iqss-cannon-quickstart-guide)

Regarding the login boxes:

1.  **VPN Box:** This is for the Cisco AnyConnect server address, which is **vpn.rc.fas.harvard.edu**. You use this to establish a secure connection to the Harvard network before accessing the cluster.
2.  **Cluster Login Box:** This is where you enter your FASRC username to log into the Cannon cluster itself.

For detailed steps on setting up your IQSS Cannon account and logging in, you can refer to the [IQSS Cannon Quickstart Guide](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/iqss-cannon-quickstart-guide).

question_59.question: My pandas script keeps blowing up with a memory error because the file is bigger than the node's RAM. Does FASRC want me to rewrite it, or can I keep using pandas somehow?
question_59.reference_answer: Both options exist, and which one FASRC recommends depends on scale. Start with chunking. For moderately large datasets, Dask can enhance Pandas by parallelizing operations — you can convert a Pandas DataFrame to a Dask DataFrame with dd.from_pandas() and keep most of your existing code. But for very large datasets that exceed memory constraints, using Dask alone as a substitute for Pandas is the more effective solution: Dask is a drop-in replacement with a familiar DataFrame API that works lazily, breaking work into smaller tasks that only execute when you call .compute(). Separately, switching from CSV to a columnar format like Parquet (e.g. df.to_parquet('output_data.parquet', compression='snappy')) greatly improves I/O performance.
question_59.answer:
You don’t need to rewrite your script from scratch, but you **do** need to change how you load the data. Pandas loads entire DataFrames into RAM, so if the file is larger than your node’s memory, you’ll get an OOM (Out-Of-Memory) error.

### What to do instead

1. **Use `chunksize` in `pd.read_csv()`**  
   This lets you process the file in smaller pieces:
   ```python
   for chunk in pd.read_csv('large_file.csv', chunksize=100_000):
       # process each chunk
       result = process(chunk)
   ```

2. **Consider Dask for larger-than-memory data**  
   Dask provides a pandas-like API but processes data in parallel and can handle datasets larger than RAM. It’s available as a Python module on FASRC clusters.

3. **Request more memory in your SLURM job**  
   If your data *can* fit in memory, request a node with enough RAM:
   ```bash
   #SBATCH --mem=64G   # or higher, depending on your data size
   ```
   Check available memory partitions and node sizes on the FASRC documentation site.

### FASRC resources
- FASRC provides example SLURM scripts for Python/pandas jobs: [Example2/run.sbatch](https://github.com/fasrc/User_Codes/blob/master/Languages/Python/Example2/run.sbatch)
- General Python setup info: [Python Programming Language – FASRC DOCS](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/python)

### Next step
Would you like help converting your script to use `chunksize`, or are you interested in setting up a Dask-based workflow?

question_60.question: I switched to the newest Intel module on the cluster and now the compiler command I've always used doesn't exist anymore. What am I supposed to call to build my C file now?
question_60.reference_answer: Intel renamed the compiler binaries at version 24.0.0. For Intel modules below 24.0.0 the commands are icc (C), ifortran (Fortran), and icpc (C++). For Intel 24.0.0 and above they are icx (C), ifx (Fortran), and icpx (C++). So with a newer Intel module you must invoke icx instead of icc. (You can list the available Intel compilers with `module spider intel` and load a specific one, e.g. `module load intel/23.0.0-fasrc01`.)
question_60.answer:
Based on the documentation, when you load the newest Intel module (e.g., `intel/23.0.0-fasrc01`), the compiler command is still `icc` for C compilation. You can verify this by running:

```bash
module load intel/23.0.0-fasrc01
which icc
```

This should return something like `/n/sw/intel-oneapi-2023/compiler/2023.0.0/linux/bin/intel64/icc` [SPACK Package Manager](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/spack-package-manager/).

If `icc` truly doesn't exist after loading your module, you may be on a different/newer oneAPI-based module where the C compiler command changed to `icx`. Try running:

```bash
module load intel/23.0.0-fasrc01
which icx
```

If `icx` is available, use that instead of `icc` to compile your C files.

Could you share which exact Intel module version you loaded (`module list` output would help)? That way I can give you the precise command for your setup.

question_61.question: Is it fine to build my C code right after I ssh in, and should I just put the gcc line at the top of my job script so it's always fresh?
question_61.reference_answer: No on both counts. FASRC recommends jumping to a compute node to compile a C program (compilation can take a few seconds to a minute depending on the code's complexity), and specifically recommends using the `test` partition to compile and test the program before running the production job. Best practice is to compile the code separately and then use the resulting executable in your sbatch script — avoid putting the compilation command inside the sbatch script, because that recompiles the program on every submission. If you change the source, recompile separately and then resubmit the production batch job.
question_61.answer:
Based on the FASRC documentation, here's what you should know:

### 1. Don't compile on login nodes

The C programming guide recommends **jumping to a compute node** for compiling C code, as compilation can take seconds to a minute depending on complexity [C Programming Language](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/c-programming-language/). It's best to use the `test` partition for compiling and testing before running production jobs.

### 2. Don't put the gcc line at the top of your sbatch script

The documentation explicitly advises: **"It is best practice to compile a C code separately and then use the executable, generated during compilation, in the production run using the sbatch script. If possible, avoid including the compilation command in the sbatch script, which will recompile the program every time the job is submitted"** [C Programming Language](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/c-programming-language/).

### Recommended workflow:

1. **Compile separately** on a compute node (e.g., via `salloc` or an interactive job on the `test` partition)
2. **Submit your production job** with `sbatch`, which should only run the already-compiled executable
3. If you change source code, recompile separately again, then resubmit

This avoids wasting compute time on recompilation and keeps your job scripts clean.

The documentation explicitly advises: **"It is best practice to compile a C code separately and then use the executable, generated during compilation, in the production run using the sbatch script. If possible, avoid including the compilation command in the sbatch script, which will recompile the program every time the job is submitted"** [C Programming Language](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/c-programming-language/).

### Recommended workflow:

1. **Compile separately** on a compute node (e.g., via `salloc` or an interactive job on the `test` partition)
2. **Submit your production job** with `sbatch`, which should only run the already-compiled executable
3. If you change source code, recompile separately again, then resubmit

This avoids wasting compute time on recompilation and keeps your job scripts clean.

question_62.question: I want to completely wipe my Julia install off the cluster and start clean. Is there a single command, and does it leave junk behind in my home directory?
question_62.reference_answer: Run `juliaup self uninstall`. That is the uninstall command, but it does not always clean everything up: afterward, check for the `~/.julia` and `~/.juliaup` directories and delete them manually if they are still there. (This matters because the default Julia install location is $HOME, and the installer also adds Juliaup initialization to your ~/.bashrc to put `julia` on your $PATH.)
question_62.answer:
There isn't a single "uninstall Julia" command documented by FASRC. The standard Julia installer for Unix (the one used on the cluster) installs to `$HOME` and adds a `juliaup` initialization line to `~/.bashrc` [Julia Programming Language – FASRC DOCS](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/julia/).

To completely wipe it, you need to do two things:

1. **Remove the installed Julia files** — the installer creates a `juliaup` directory (and possibly a `julia-<version>` directory) in your home directory. You can remove it with:
   ```bash
   rm -rf ~/.juliaup ~/.julia
   ```
   *(Adjust the exact directory names if yours differ; the installer typically creates `~/.juliaup` and `~/.julia`.)*

2. **Remove the `juliaup` line from `~/.bashrc`** — the installer adds a line like:
   ```bash
   source "$HOME/.juliaup/bin/juliaup.sh"
   ```
   You'll need to manually edit `~/.bashrc` and delete that line so `julia` doesn't reappear in your `$PATH` on next login.

**Does it leave junk behind?** Yes, if you only run `rm -rf ~/.juliaup ~/.julia` without editing `~/.bashrc`, the `julia` command will still be found because the `juliaup` initialization remains in your shell profile. Additionally, Julia packages you installed via `Pkg.add()` live in `~/.julia`, so removing that directory also cleans up those packages.

If you also installed packages via `Conda.jl` or `PyCall.jl`, those may have created additional files in `~/.julia` as well.

question_63.question: I chmod 777'd a file in my lab's share so a collaborator in a different lab group could grab it, but they still get permission denied when they try to read it. What's going on?
question_63.reference_answer: Making the file world-readable is not enough on its own. For a user in the 'Other' category to reach a file, they must first be able to traverse into the top-level share/directory that contains it. If the top level of the lab directory or share is set drwxr-x---, drwxrwx---, or drwxr-s--- then Other has no access to the share at all, even if a file inside it is set -rwxrwxrwx. Other must first be able to 'see' into the directory/share; otherwise it has no access. (FASSE/L3 shares should never allow Other access.) To share with someone outside the group, the enclosing directory must permit Other traversal - e.g. the 'Everyone' directory that lab shares provide for exactly this purpose - or the person can be added to your lab Group by your PI.
question_63.answer:
The most likely reason your collaborator still gets "permission denied" is that **the parent directory (or one of the parent directories) leading to the file does not allow `Other` users to traverse it**.

Here's how POSIX permissions work in this scenario:

### The "Directory Traversal" Problem

Permissions are checked at **every level** of the path. Even if a file is set to `777` (readable by everyone), a collaborator must also have **execute (`x`) permission on every parent directory** in the path to reach it.

For example, if your lab share looks like:
```
/n/holylabs/your_lab/
├── drwxr-x---  (top-level directory)
│   └── -rwxrwxrwx  (your file)
```

The top-level directory has `---` for `Other`, meaning **no one outside your group can even enter the directory**, regardless of what permissions the file inside has.

### How to Fix It

You need to ensure that the **parent directories** also allow `Other` (or at least your collaborator's group) to traverse them. You can do this with:

```bash
chmod o+x /n/holylabs/your_lab
```

Or, if you want to be more permissive on the directory itself:

```bash
chmod o+rx /n/holylabs/your_lab
```

Then verify with `ls -ld /n/holylabs/your_lab` that the `Other` permissions now include `x` (and `r` if they need to list the directory contents).

### Important Notes

- **FASSE/L3 shares should never allow `Other` access** ([Understanding file and group permissions](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/understanding-permissions)). If you're on those shares, you'll need a different approach.
- For sharing with external collaborators, consider using **Globus** instead, which is designed for secure file sharing without requiring system accounts ([Globus File Transfer](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/globus-file-transfer)).

question_64.question: My labmate keeps his personal scratch folder under Users/ in our old lab share, but our newly created share and netscratch have no Users folder. Where am I supposed to put my own personal directory now?
question_64.reference_answer: The Users directory only exists on shares created prior to October 2024. On new shares and on /n/netscratch there is no Users directory - FASRC says to use the Lab directory to create personal folders instead. The Lab directory is set drwxrws--- so that every member of the lab group has read/write/execute access to share data amongst the group, and it is the preferred place both for personal folders on new shares and for sharing data with your lab group. On the older shares, the sub-directories in the Users directory are owned by individuals and by default only allow execute access to the group.
question_64.answer:
Based on the available documentation, I cannot find specific information about the old `Users/` folder structure in lab shares or where personal directories should be placed in newly created shares and netscratch.

Here's what I can tell you from the retrieved sources:

**For Lab Storage:**
- The Lab directory is intended as the primary working directory and is shared via Globus [Data Storage (Offerings, Workflow, Costs)](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/data-storage-workflow-rdm/).
- Individual users may update their permissions to adjust access as they like, though keeping access open to all lab members is recommended for easier collaboration [Data Storage (Offerings, Workflow, Costs)](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/data-storage-workflow-rdm/).

**For Netscratch:**
- Netscratch (`/n/netscratch`) is maintained as a large, shared temporary scratch filesystem for high I/O jobs [Scratch – FASRC DOCS](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/policy-scratch).
- Each lab is allotted 50TB of scratch space, but files older than 90 days will be deleted through a periodic purge process [Scratch – FASRC DOCS](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/policy-scratch).
- Netscratch is volatile, temporary space for transient data and is *not backed up* [Scratch – FASRC DOCS](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/policy-scratch).

**Recommendation:**
Since the documentation doesn't cover the specific `Users/` folder deprecation or the new share structure, I'd recommend:
1. Checking with your lab's PI or admin about the new directory structure
2. Looking at the Storage Modernization Initiative FAQs for information about changes to lab storage [Storage Modernization Initiative: Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/storage-modernization-initiative-faqs)
3. Contacting FASRC support directly for guidance on the new share structure

question_65.question: I finished the cluster account request form and it never asked me to choose a password. How do I actually get a password to log in?
question_65.reference_answer: Passwords are not collected by the signup application. Your account is created with a random password, and upon completion of the request you use the password reset tool to set your initial password. You will receive an email once the account has been created with links and instructions to do so.
question_65.answer:
That's expected — the account request form doesn't ask you to create a password. Instead, you set it **after** your account is approved. Here's how:

1. **Go to the RC password reset link:** <https://portal.rc.fas.harvard.edu/p3/pwreset/>
2. **Enter the email address** you used when signing up for your account.
3. **Check your email** for a one-time-use link (it expires after 15 minutes).
4. **Click the link** and set your password.

Once you've set your password, you'll also need to set up **OpenAuth two-factor authentication (2FA)** before you can log in. See the [OpenAuth Guide](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/openauth/) for instructions.

For full details, see the [User Quick Start Guide](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/quickstart-guide/).

question_66.question: I log into the FASRC web portal in my browser, it accepts my credentials, and then it just spins forever and never shows the menus. Restarting the browser doesn't help. What can I do myself before emailing support?
question_66.reference_answer:
If the browser hangs for a long time after authenticating without displaying the Open OnDemand dashboard, restart your Per-User NGINX (PUN) process by visiting:
- Cannon: https://rcood.rc.fas.harvard.edu/nginx/stop?redir=/pun/sys/dashboard/
- FASSE: https://fasseood.rc.fas.harvard.edu/nginx/stop?redir=/pun/sys/dashboard/
Also note that the very first login can legitimately take some time while OOD sets up files and cache in your home directory; that Avast security software can cause 'no internet', 'read error', and 'the requested URL could not be retrieved' messages (disable Web Shield); and that Chrome or Firefox are recommended over Safari and Internet Explorer.
question_66.answer:
Based on the FASRC documentation, here are the steps you can take to troubleshoot a spinning/frozen Open OnDemand (OOD) dashboard before contacting support:

### 1. Check if this is your first login
If this is your **first time** logging into the Open OnDemand dashboard, it can take a while to set up files and cache in your home directory. If you just logged in for the first time, give it a few more minutes to finish initializing.

### 2. Clear your browser cache and cookies
Stale or corrupted browser cache and cookies are a common cause of dashboards that spin forever after accepting credentials. Try:
*   **Clear your browser's cache and cookies** for the OOD site (e.g., `rcood.rc.fas.harvard.edu` or `fasseood.rc.fas.harvard.edu`).
*   Alternatively, try opening the dashboard in an **incognito/private window** to bypass any existing cache/cookies.

### 3. Try a different browser
FASRC recommends using **[Chrome](https://www.google.com/chrome/)** or **[Firefox](https://www.mozilla.org/en-US/firefox/)** for the best experience. Safari and Internet Explorer may not work as expected for some dashboard apps. If you're using one of those, try switching to Chrome or Firefox.

### 4. Verify your VPN connection
Make sure you are connected to the **FASRC VPN** before accessing the dashboard. Cluster users should connect using the `@fasrc` realm (e.g., `jharvard@fasrc`), while FASSE (including NCF) users should use the `@fasse` realm (e.g., `jharvard@fasse`).

### 5. Check the status page
The dashboard includes a link to the FASRC status page. You can check if there are any known outages or maintenance events affecting the OOD service.

If none of these steps resolve the issue, you may want to email FASRC support with details about your browser, whether this is your first login, and any error messages you see in the browser's developer console.

question_67.question: My R job asks Slurm for 8 cores, but when it runs my parallel code spawns dozens of workers and the node grinds to a halt. How am I supposed to determine the worker count inside the script?
question_67.reference_answer: Do not use parallel::detectCores() to determine the number of CPUs/processes to use in your job - it detects the number of physical CPU cores on the compute node, not the number allocated to your job, which is why you end up oversubscribed. Use parallelly::availableCores() instead, which returns the number of CPUs allocated to your Slurm job.
question_67.answer:
The problem you're seeing is a classic oversubscription: Slurm allocates 8 cores to your job, but your R parallel code doesn't know that limit and defaults to spawning workers equal to the **total physical cores on the node**, which can be dozens.

### How to detect the correct worker count in R

Slurm sets environment variables that your script can read. The key ones are:

- **`SLURM_NTASKS`** — the number of tasks (MPI-style processes) allocated to your job. If you used `#SBATCH --ntasks=8`, this will be `8`.
- **`SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK`** — the number of CPUs allocated per task. If you used `#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1`, this will be `1`.
- **`SLURM_NCPUS`** or **`SLURM_JOB_CPUS_PER_NODE`** — total CPUs on the node (not recommended for limiting workers, since it reflects the whole node, not your allocation).

For a typical R parallel job where you want one worker per allocated core, the safest approach is to read `SLURM_NTASKS` (or `SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK` × `SLURM_NTASKS` if you allocated multiple CPUs per task).

### Example in R

```r
# Read the number of workers from Slurm
n_workers <- as.integer(Sys.getenv("SLURM_NTASKS"))

# Fallback if running interactively (not on Slurm)
if (is.na(n_workers) || n_workers == 0) {
  n_workers <- parallel::detectCores(logical = TRUE)
}

# Use it with your parallel backend
library(parallel)
cl <- makeCluster(n_workers)
```

Or, if you allocated multiple CPUs per task and want to use them all:

```r
n_workers <- as.integer(Sys.getenv("SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK")) *
             as.integer(Sys.getenv("SLURM_NTASKS"))
```

### Why this works

Slurm sets `SLURM_NTASKS` and `SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK` as environment variables in every job step, so your R script can read them at runtime. This ensures your parallel code respects the resources you asked for, rather than guessing based on the node's total hardware.

### Quick check

You can verify these variables are set by running this in your job script before launching R:

```bash
echo "SLURM_NTASKS=$SLURM_NTASKS"
echo "SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK"
```

If you're using a specific parallel package (e.g., `parallel`, `future`, `doParallel`, `foreach`), let me know and I can give you the exact syntax for that package.

question_68.question: I had openmpi loaded, then loaded mpich later in the same session, and now openmpi is gone from my module list. Did I corrupt my environment, and can I keep both around?
question_68.reference_answer: Nothing is corrupted - this is intentional. The modules are set up so that you can only have one MPI module loaded at a time; if you try loading a second one it will automatically unload the first, which is done to avoid dependency collisions. So you cannot keep both loaded: pick one implementation (OpenMPI or MPICH, each built with either the GNU or the Intel compiler suite) and load it with its matching compiler module, e.g. module load gcc/13.2.0-fasrc01 openmpi/5.0.2-fasrc01. Note also that there is no default MPI library in your environment when you log in - you must load one.
question_68.answer:
No, you haven't corrupted your environment — this is expected behavior. On the FASRC cluster, **MPI implementations (OpenMPI and MPICH) are mutually exclusive** because they provide the same set of commands and libraries (e.g., `mpicc`, `mpirun`, `libmpi.so`). Loading one will replace the other in your environment.

This is by design, not a bug. The cluster uses Lmod, which manages module conflicts by unloading conflicting modules when you load a new one.

### Can you keep both around?

You can't have both loaded simultaneously in the same shell session, but you can:

1. **Switch between them** by unloading one and loading the other:
   ```bash
   module unload mpich
   module load openmpi/5.0.2-fasrc01
   ```

2. **Load both in a job script** — each job gets its own environment, so you can specify whichever MPI implementation your job needs at submission time.

3. **Use conda environments** with their own bundled MPI libraries (e.g., `mpi4py` installed via `mamba` pulls in MPICH by default, but you can also install OpenMPI-backed versions). This isolates MPI from the system modules entirely.

For reproducibility, it's recommended to use the full module name (e.g., `openmpi/5.0.2-fasrc01`) rather than just `openmpi` [MPI (Message Passing Interface) & OpenMPI](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/mpi-message-passing-interface/).

question_69.reference_answer: Putting mpi4py in the mamba create package list (e.g. mamba create -n python3_env1 python numpy pip wheel mpi4py) also installs an MPI library required by mpi4py, and by default that is MPICH - not OpenMPI. If your workflow requires a specific flavor and/or version of MPI, install mpi4py with pip into a custom conda environment instead: load the compiler and MPI modules first (module load gcc/12.2.0-fasrc01; module load openmpi/4.1.5-fasrc03), load a Python module (module load python/3.10.12-fasrc01), create the environment WITHOUT mpi4py (mamba create -n python3_env2 python numpy pip wheel), activate it (source activate python3_env2), then run pip install mpi4py so it builds against the loaded OpenMPI.

question_70.question: I used the 'copy mount path to clipboard' button in Starfish and got /n/vast-holylabs/C/jharvard_lab, but when I cd to it on a login node I get 'No such file or directory'. What's the correct path?
question_70.reference_answer: The path Starfish copies is not directly usable - you must make two edits: remove 'vast-' and remove '/C'. So /n/vast-holylabs/C/jharvard_lab becomes /n/holylabs/jharvard_lab. The letter C indicates the filesystem is on the Cannon cluster; a group share on FASSE would show F instead of C before the group name.
question_70.answer:
The path `/n/vast-holylabs/C/jharvard_lab` is a **Starfish internal path** used by the Starfish dashboard to identify the storage location — it is **not** a filesystem path you can `cd` to on a login node or compute node.

The correct path for your lab's holylabs storage on the cluster is:

```
/n/holylabs/jharvard_lab
```

This is confirmed by the FASRC storage documentation, which states that the Lab Directory (holylabs) is located at `/n/holylabs` [Getting Started with FASRC Storage](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/getting-started-with-fasrc-storage/).

You can verify this by running:

```bash
ls /n/holylabs/jharvard_lab
```

If you need to access this storage from your local desktop or laptop, note that holylabs **cannot** be mounted via Samba/SMB — you'll need to use SCP, SFTP, or Globus instead [Mounting Storage on Desktop or Laptop](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/mounting-storage/).

question_71.question: I want to drag a few files out of my home directory into my lab's netscratch folder using a point-and-click interface, but my home directory doesn't show up as an endpoint in Globus. What else can I use?
question_71.reference_answer: Globus does not have access to home directories, which is why yours does not appear. For transfers to or from your home directory, use an Open OnDemand Remote Desktop session instead: go to the OOD dashboard (Cannon: rcood.rc.fas.harvard.edu, FASSE: fasseood.rc.fas.harvard.edu), start a Remote Desktop session, open a File Manager by clicking the 'Home' folder on the desktop (or Applications -> File Manager), open a second File Manager window, navigate one to the source (e.g. /n/home01/jharvard/) and the other to the destination (e.g. /n/netscratch/jharvard_lab/Lab/), then right-click the source file -> Copy and right-click the destination window -> Paste (drag-and-drop works too, but behaves like cut-and-paste). Command-line tools (cp, mv, rsync, fpsync) are the alternative; Globus is only recommended for transfers between different filesystems, not within one.
question_71.answer:
Your home directory is intentionally excluded from Globus for security reasons — it can expose authentication keys and passwords if shared.

For point-and-click transfers of files from your home directory to your lab's netscratch folder, you have a few options:

1. **Use Globus via your Lab directory** — Globus can see folders inside your lab share (e.g., `/n/holylabs/<lab_name>/Lab`). You can copy files from your home directory to the lab share first (using `cp` or `rsync` on the cluster), then drag them out via Globus from the lab share.

2. **Use `scp` or `rsync` over SSH** — These are the standard alternatives to Globus for transferring files to/from your home directory. For example:
   ```bash
   scp -r /path/to/local/files username@cluster.fas.harvard.edu:/home/username/
   ```
   Or from the cluster to your local machine:
   ```bash
   scp -r username@cluster.fas.harvard.edu:/home/username/file.txt /local/path/
   ```

3. **Use Globus Connect Personal** — If you want a point-and-click interface on your local machine, you can install [Globus Connect Personal](https://docs.globus.org/how-to/get-started/#the_transfer_files_page) on your local computer. This creates a local endpoint that you can drag-and-drop files to/from, and then transfer them to/from the cluster via Globus.

For more details on Globus, see [Globus File Transfer](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/globus-file-transfer/).

question_72.question: My collaborator is at another university and doesn't have a HarvardKey. Can she still get an account on the cluster, and is there anything I have to keep doing so her access doesn't get shut off?
question_72.reference_answer: Yes. A collaborator without a HarvardKey can apply for an external FASRC account through the account request portal (https://portal.rc.fas.harvard.edu/request/account). External accounts have to be re-enabled every 90 days: the PI must request an extension every 90 days or the account will be suspended. Faculty can sponsor FASRC accounts for anyone working in their lab, including external collaborators.
question_72.answer:
Yes, your collaborator can get an account even without a HarvardKey. According to FASRC's account qualifications:

- **If she is a faculty member at another university** collaborating with a Harvard PI, she should choose **EXTERNAL** status during sign-up.
- **If she is a student or researcher at another university or company** collaborating with a Harvard PI, she should also choose **EXTERNAL** status.

She will need to be sponsored/authorized by a Harvard PI or management to get the account approved.

### Ongoing requirements to keep her access active:

1. **She must remain subscribed to the FASRC notifications mailing list** — this is a requirement for all users.
2. **She must continue to use the account for legitimate research purposes** that benefit Harvard University's research projects.
3. **She is held accountable** by Harvard University's Electronic Access and Information Security policies.

The Harvard PI sponsoring her account is responsible for ensuring her access remains appropriate. If you'd like more details on the account request process, you can find it at [Request an FAS RC Account](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/how-do-i-get-a-research-computing-account/).

question_73.question: I'm a new PI with a HarvardKey but the system won't let me approve my grad student's FASRC account request. What do I need to do?
question_73.reference_answer: Complete the FAS Onboard tool for approvers at https://onboard.rc.fas.harvard.edu/onboard/. The onboarding checklist states that if you have a HarvardKey but are denied access to approve new accounts, you should visit and complete the FAS Onboard tool for approvers.
question_73.answer:
It sounds like your PI profile isn't yet recognized in the FASRC portal, so the system can't link you to your grad student's request. Here's what to do:

1. **Confirm your PI status in the portal**
   - Log in to the [FAS RC & Informatics Portal](https://portal.rc.fas.harvard.edu/) with your HarvardKey.
   - Go to the **PI Management** section and verify that your lab group(s) and affiliations are listed. If they're missing or incorrect, you'll need to add or update them there.

2. **Ensure your PI account is fully vetted**
   - If you selected **NON-FACULTY PI** during signup (or if your faculty appointment isn't yet reflected), your account and PI rights require vetting by FASRC staff before you can approve requests. FASRC may contact you for additional information.

3. **Check your grad student's request**
   - Once your PI profile is active, your grad student's request should appear in your portal dashboard for approval. Make sure they selected you as their PI/sponsor when they submitted their request.

4. **If it still doesn't work**
   - Contact FASRC directly for help updating your PI profile or resolving the approval issue.

For more details, see the [Cluster Account Signup](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/account-signup/) and [Account Qualifications and Affiliations](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/account-qualifications/) pages.

question_74.question: We're wrapping up a project and want to push the raw data off to tape. Before we start, what constraints are there on how the data has to be laid out, and what does it cost per year?
question_74.reference_answer: Tape (NESE) storage is sold in 20TB increments, allows ten thousand files per folder, and requires file sizes between 1GiB and 100GiB. It costs $15/yr per TB, is externally managed by the Northeast Storage Exchange (NESE), and data is transferred to tape using Globus. It is intended for long-term storage of inactive research data after project completion or for data retention purposes.
question_74.answer:
Based on the FASRC documentation, here's what you need to know about tape storage:

## Constraints on Data Layout

1. **Tar archives recommended** — You should create `tar` archives of your data rather than copying raw files directly. The documentation recommends breaking large datasets into smaller archives (e.g., 50–200 GB each) to reduce the risk of total data loss from corruption [Tips for using tar to archive data](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/tips-for-tar-archiving/).

2. **File count limits** — Tape allocations have file count limits based on size. For example, a 200 TB allocation has a default limit of 2,000,000 files (200 TB / 100 MB) [Starfish Zones Data Visualization Tool](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/starfish-data-management/).

3. **Single directory requirement** — If using `tar`, your data should be contained within the same directory; the archiving approach assumes a single directory tree [Tips for using tar to archive data](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/tips-for-tar-archiving/).

4. **Checksums recommended** — Create checksums (e.g., SHA-1) of your archives to verify integrity when retrieving data later [Tips for using tar to archive data](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/tips-for-tar-archiving/).

5. **Access via Globus only** — Tape storage cannot be mounted or accessed via SSH/SCP/SFTP; it is only accessible via Globus [Mounting Storage on Desktop or Laptop](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/mounting-storage/).

6. **Permissions** — Only the PI and General Manager have default access to tape via Globus; they must explicitly share access with other lab members [Globus: Transfer Data to Tape](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/tape-globus-access/).

## Cost

The documentation references that tape storage is a paid offering managed through the Storage Service Center and allocated via Coldfront, but the specific per-TiB annual rate for tape storage is not provided in the retrieved documents. You can request a tape allocation through the [Coldfront Allocation Dashboard](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/coldfront-allocation-management/) and contact the Storage Service Center for current pricing [Storage Modernization Initiative: FAQs](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/storage-modernization-initiative-faqs/).

For billing details, charges are based on allocation size (TiB) and storage offering, billed monthly based on annual rates [Data Storage Billing](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/data-storage-billing/).

Would you like help with the next steps, such as requesting a tape allocation or preparing your data for archiving?

question_75.question: I put a dataset in the Everyone folder so another lab could grab it, but it never shows up in Globus. Is Globus broken?
question_75.reference_answer: No, that is expected behavior. The Everyone subdirectory is visible to anyone on the HPC cluster and is intended only for internal sharing with other labs on the cluster — it is not available on Globus. The Lab subdirectory is the one shared out via Globus, so data that has to move over Globus needs to live under Lab.
question_75.answer:
Globus isn't broken—files placed in the **Everyone** folder simply **do not sync to Globus**. According to FASRC documentation, the Everyone directory is "intended only for internal sharing" and is explicitly **not available on Globus** [Data Storage (Offerings, Workflow, Costs)](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/data-storage-workflow-rdm/).

Globus only exposes the **Lab** folder (and other designated shared collections) for external collaboration. If you want another lab to access your data via Globus, you'll need to move or copy the dataset into your lab's Globus-shared directory instead.

question_76.question: Is there already a samtools container sitting on the cluster somewhere, or do I have to pull one from Docker Hub myself?
question_76.reference_answer: There is one already on the cluster. Cluster nodes automount a CernVM-File System at /cvmfs/singularity.galaxyproject.org/, which provides Singularity images for the BioContainers project (auto-generated from Bioconda packages). Images follow the layout /cvmfs/singularity.galaxyproject.org/FIRST_LETTER/SECOND_LETTER/PACKAGE_NAME:VERSION--CONDA_BUILD, for example: `singularity exec /cvmfs/singularity.galaxyproject.org/s/a/samtools:1.13--h8c37831_0 samtools --help`. Expect a 10-30 second delay the first time the path is accessed on a compute node that has not mounted/cached it.
question_76.answer:
Based on the available documentation, there is no pre-installed samtools container on the FASRC cluster. You will need to pull/build one yourself.

Here are your options:

1.  **Pull from Docker Hub and convert to Singularity:** You can build a Singularity image from an OCI container image located in Docker Hub or another registry using `singularity build` [Singularity – FASRC DOCS](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/singularity-on-the-cluster/).
2.  **Download an existing Singularity image:** You can download an existing Singularity image from the SingularityCE Container Library or another image repository [Singularity – FASRC DOCS](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/singularity-on-the-cluster/).

For running containers on the cluster, Singularity is recommended for ease of use in an HPC environment [AlphaFold – FASRC DOCS](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/alphafold/).

question_77.question: A spack install blew up and by the time I looked the build log was already gone. How do I stop spack from throwing the logs away?
question_77.reference_answer: Spack builds in a `stage` directory located in /tmp and cleans that space up once it finishes building, whether the build succeeded or failed — which is why the logs disappear. To keep them, first set the `$TMP` environment variable to a location you want the stage files dumped into, then add the `--keep-stage` flag, e.g. `spack install --keep-stage <package>`, which tells spack to keep the staging files rather than remove them.
question_77.answer:
Spack automatically deletes build logs after a successful install, but you can prevent that with the `--keep-build-tree` flag or by setting a config option.

**Quick fix for a single install:**
```bash
spack install --keep-build-tree <package>
```

**Permanent fix via config:**
Add this to your `~/.spack/config.yaml` (or the site-wide config):
```yaml
config:
  build_logs_root: /path/to/keep/logs
  install_keep_tree: true
```

- `install_keep_tree: true` tells Spack not to remove the build tree (and its logs) after a successful install.
- `build_logs_root` lets you point logs to a specific directory if you want them organized separately.

You can also find logs for a *failed* install in `~/.spack/logs/` — Spack only deletes logs on **success**, so if the install actually failed, the logs should still be there.

question_78.question: Software I built with spack runs fine on the node I built it on but won't run on nodes in other partitions. How do I build something that works everywhere on the cluster?
question_78.reference_answer:
By default Spack autodetects the architecture of the hardware it is building on and optimizes the build for it, so a build made on one CPU generation may not run on another (the docs give the example that LAMMPS built on Sapphire Rapids may not run on Cascade Lake). If you plan to run across heterogeneous hardware/partitions, set Spack to a generic architecture: edit `etc/spack/packages.yaml` inside the spack folder (create it if it does not exist) and add:
packages:
  all:
    target: [x86_64]
question_78.answer:
The issue you're experiencing is likely due to **architecture-specific optimizations** in your Spack build. When Spack compiles software, it may target the specific CPU architecture of the node where you built it, which can cause binaries to fail on nodes with different CPU types or microarchitectures.

To build software that works across all nodes on the cluster, you should:

1. **Use a portable target architecture** when building with Spack. Instead of targeting the specific CPU of your build node, specify a more general architecture that's compatible with all cluster nodes.

2. **Check your cluster's CPU architecture** to determine the most portable target. On FASRC clusters, this is typically something like `x86_64` or a specific generation that's common across all nodes.

3. **Use Spack's `target` specification** in your build command. For example:
   ```bash
   spack install --target=x86_64 your_package
   ```
   Or in your Spack environment/config, you can specify the target architecture.

4. **Avoid overly aggressive optimization flags** that target specific CPU features. You can control compiler flags through Spack's configuration.

For detailed guidance on Spack configuration and architecture targeting, refer to the [SPACK Package Manager documentation](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/spack-package-manager/).

question_79.question: I don't want spack spending hours compiling its own OpenMPI — how do I make it use the openmpi module we already have on the cluster, and is there anything I have to do before installing?
question_79.reference_answer:
Configure the cluster's OpenMPI as an external package in `~/.spack/packages.yaml` (create the file if it does not exist). Get the prefix by loading the modules and reading $MPI_HOME, then add:
packages:
  openmpi:
    externals:
    - spec: openmpi@5.0.5%gcc@14.2.0
      prefix: /n/sw/helmod-rocky8/apps/Comp/gcc/14.2.0-fasrc01/openmpi/5.0.5-fasrc01
    buildable: false
The `buildable: false` option ensures MPI won't be built from source and Spack will use the module in that prefix instead. Before installing, run `module purge` — this is required or the build fails (e.g. `module purge` then `spack install hdf5@1.14.6 % gcc@14.2.0 ^ openmpi@5.0.5`).
question_79.answer:
To make Spack use the cluster's existing `openmpi` module instead of compiling its own, you need to tell Spack to treat it as an **external package**. Here's how:

### 1. Load the module first
Before running any Spack commands, load the OpenMPI module you want Spack to use:

```bash
module load openmpi/<version>-fasrcXX
```

### 2. Discover external packages
Run `spack external find` to have Spack scan your environment for already-installed software (including modules):

```bash
spack external find
```

This will detect the loaded OpenMPI module and add it to your `~/.spack/packages.yaml` file as an external package [Spack Package Manager – FASRC DOCS](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/spack).

### 3. Verify and optionally lock it
Check that Spack sees the external OpenMPI:

```bash
spack find openmpi
```

If you want to **prevent Spack from ever building its own OpenMPI**, add a `buildable: false` entry for it in your `~/.spack/packages.yaml`:

```yaml
packages:
  openmpi:
    externals:
      - spec: openmpi@<version>
        prefix: /n/sw/helmod-rocky8/apps/MPI/gcc/<compiler>/openmpi/<version>
    buildable: false
```

You can find the correct `prefix` path by running `module show openmpi/<version>` or `which mpirun` after loading the module.

### Key point
As the docs note, Spack will normally build its own package stack even if libraries are available on the system. You **must** have the module loaded *before* running `spack external find` for it to be detected [Spack Package Manager – FASRC DOCS](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/spack).

question_80.question: We cleaned out several TB of old data last month but this month's storage charge came in exactly the same. Is the bill wrong?
question_80.reference_answer: No, the bill is correct. The monthly charge is based on the size of the storage allocation, not on the amount of storage actually used, so deleting files will not reduce the charge unless the allocation size itself is also reduced. Separately, the cutoff for billing changes is the 15th of each month — any change made to an allocation after the 15th is only reflected on the following month's bill.
question_80.answer:
The bill is likely correct. According to FASRC's [Data Storage Billing](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/data-storage-billing/) documentation:

> The monthly charge for RC Storage is based on the storage tier and the **total size of the allocation**, not the amount of used space. As a result, **deleting files will not reduce your monthly cost unless the allocation size is also reduced**.

In other words, storage charges are based on how much storage you've been allocated (e.g., 10 TiB), not how much of it you're actually using. Deleting old data frees up space, but it doesn't change the size of your allocation — so the bill stays the same.

If you want to reduce your storage costs, you'd need to **reduce the allocation size** itself. Keep in mind that billing changes are determined on the **15th of each month**, so any changes made after that date won't be reflected until the following month's bill.

If you believe there's an error on your bill, you can contact [RC Storage Billing](mailto:billing@rc.fas.harvard.edu) within 3 business days of receiving the notification.

question_82.question: Every time I try to map my Cannon home drive on my Windows laptop I end up locked out of my account. How many bad tries does that take, how long am I locked out for, and what am I doing wrong in the Map Network Drive box?
question_82.reference_answer: You are almost certainly letting Windows authenticate with your local PC account. In the Map Network Drive dialog you must tick "Connect using different credentials"; if you don't, Windows tries your local PC information and after three failed attempts you are locked out. The lockout expires automatically in about 5 minutes. When prompted for network credentials, prepend your FASRC username with RC\ (for example RC\jharvard) so you authenticate against the RC domain.
question_82.answer:
Based on the FASRC documentation, here is what is happening:

### How many bad tries and how long is the lockout?
According to the [Locked Account](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/unlock_account/) guide, your account locks after entering the incorrect password **multiple times**. The lockout is not permanent and will **automatically unlock after about 5–10 minutes**. If it remains locked longer than that, you should contact FASRC support.

### What you are doing wrong
The most common reason for repeated lockouts when mapping a network drive is an incorrect username format. When prompted for credentials in the **Map Network Drive** box on Windows, you must prepend your FASRC username with the **`RC\`** domain specifier.

*   **Incorrect:** `your_username`
*   **Correct:** `RC\your_username`

### Correct steps to map your Cannon home drive
1.  **Connect to the VPN:** Cluster storage must be routed through the Research Computing VPN.
2.  **Find your home directory path:** SSH into Cannon and run `cd ~` to see your home directory path (e.g., `/n/home13/your_username`). The folder name (e.g., `home13`) is the part you need.
3.  **Map the drive:**
    *   Open File Explorer and select **This PC**.
    *   Click **Map network drive** and choose a drive letter.
    *   In the **Folder** box, enter the path: `\\rcstore.rc.fas.harvard.edu\homes\homeXX\your_username` (replace `homeXX` with your actual home directory folder, like `home13`).
    *   When prompted for credentials, enter **`RC\your_username`** as the username and your FASRC password.

For more details, see the [Mounting Storage on Desktop or Laptop](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/mounting-storage/) guide.

question_83.question: I'm on a collaborator's network where I can't run a second VPN client. Can I still get files off the cluster with FileZilla, or is the VPN mandatory for everything?
question_83.reference_answer: You can still use SFTP. Mounting cluster storage as a drive does require the VPN — cluster storage must be routed through a VPN connection — but SFTP to a login node does not require a FASRC/FAS VPN connection, because login nodes use two-factor authentication. FASRC recommends FileZilla as a cross-platform SFTP client; you need OpenAuth set up plus cluster access and a home directory.
question_83.answer:
**Yes, you can use FileZilla without the VPN** — the FASRC documentation explicitly states that if you are just SSH'ing (or using SFTP via FileZilla) to the login nodes, **VPN is not required** [VPN Setup](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/vpn-setup/).

The VPN is mandatory only for specific services like:
* Mounting shared drives to your laptop/desktop
* Accessing Open OnDemand (VDI)
* Accessing level 3 environments
* License server access
* Accessing Starfish

For standard SFTP file transfers using FileZilla, you can connect directly to the login nodes:
* **Cannon:** `login.rc.fas.harvard.edu`
* **FASSE:** `fasselogin.rc.fas.harvard.edu`

Just make sure you use **SFTP – SSH File Transfer Protocol** with **Interactive** login type so you're prompted for your OpenAuth token [SFTP file transfer using Filezilla (Mac/Windows/Linux)](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/sftp-file-transfer/).

question_84.question: My home dir is full and now rm won't even work — it says 'No space left on device' when I try to delete something. How am I supposed to clean up if I can't delete anything?
question_84.reference_answer: Shrink a file to zero bytes instead of unlinking it. Pick a large file you intend to remove and run `truncate -s 0 FILENAME` (you can list several files: `truncate -s 0 FILE1 FILE2 FILE3`), or equivalently redirect the empty device into it with `cat /dev/null > ~/mybig.file`. Once enough space is recovered to get you back under quota, `rm` will work again. Use full paths when deleting to avoid removing the wrong file.
question_84.answer:
This is a known edge case: when your home directory is over quota, the filesystem won't let you allocate new blocks, so even `rm` can fail with **"No space left on device"** because the deletion operation itself needs a tiny bit of free space to update directory metadata.

### Workaround: truncate files to zero bytes first

Instead of deleting, shrink the largest files to 0 bytes using `truncate`:

```bash
truncate -s 0 ~/path/to/bigfile.out
```

Or, if `truncate` also fails:

```bash
cat /dev/null > ~/path/to/bigfile
```

Once you've freed enough space to get **under quota**, `rm` will work normally again.

### Find what's using space

```bash
cd ~
du -h --max-depth=1 .
```

If `df` says you're over quota but `du` shows less, you may have **sparse files**. In that case, use:

```bash
du -ch --apparent-size --max-depth=1 .
```

### Watch out for `~/.local`

The `~/.local` folder often balloons from `pip install` outside virtual environments. If it's the culprit, stop any running jobs (`squeue -u <username>`), then rename it:

```bash
mv ~/.local ~/.local.bak
```

This frees space immediately; you can recreate a clean `.local` later.

Let me know if you'd like help identifying the biggest files or directories to target.

question_85.question: Quota says I'm at my limit but when I add up my folders with du it's way less than that. Which one is lying, and how do I find whatever is eating the space?
question_85.reference_answer: Neither is lying — you likely have sparse files, whose space is counted by the filesystem's quota check (what `df` reports) but not accounted for properly by `du`. To find them, show the logical size instead: `cd ~` then `du -ch --apparent-size --max-depth=1 .` That points you at the directories responsible.
question_85.answer:
**Neither is necessarily lying** — the discrepancy is usually caused by one of two things:

### 1. Deleted files still held open by running processes
When a file is deleted (`rm`) but a process still has it open, the space isn't freed until the process closes it or restarts. You can check for this with:

```bash
lsof +L1
```

This lists files that have been deleted but are still held open. Restarting the relevant job/process will free the space.

### 2. Sparse files
Sparse files are files that appear large in `du`'s default output but don't actually consume that much disk space. The filesystem quota tracks the *actual* allocated blocks, not the apparent size. To see the true picture, use:

```bash
du -ch --apparent-size --max-depth=1 .
```

This shows the **logical/apparent size** rather than the disk blocks used, which should align more closely with what `quota` reports.

### How to find what's eating space
Once you know which directory is the culprit:

```bash
cd ~
du -h --max-depth=1 .
```

Then drill down into the largest directories to find specific files. For hidden folders like `~/.local` (which can grow from `pip install` outside of virtual environments), check those as well.

### If you're over quota and can't delete files
If `rm` gives "No space left on device," you can truncate files to zero bytes to free space:

```bash
truncate -s 0 FILENAME
```

Or:

```bash
cat /dev/null > FILENAME
```

Once you're under quota, you can then use `rm` normally.

question_86.question: openconnect on my Ubuntu box dies right after it authenticates — something about not being able to find a script to configure the tunnel. How do I fix that?
question_86.reference_answer: OpenConnect needs vpnc-script. Install it if you don't have it (Ubuntu/Debian: `sudo apt-get install vpnc-scripts`; Fedora/CentOS: `sudo dnf install vpnc-script`; Arch: `sudo pacman -S vpnc`), make sure it is executable (e.g. `sudo chmod u+x /etc/vpnc/vpnc-script`), and if OpenConnect still can't find it, pass its location explicitly: `openconnect --script /etc/vpnc/vpnc-script https://vpn.rc.fas.harvard.edu/` (substituting the actual path on your system).
question_86.answer:
The error you're seeing is because OpenConnect can't find the **vpnc-script** that configures the tunnel after authentication. Here's how to fix it:

1. **Install the vpnc-script package** (if you don't already have it):
   ```bash
   sudo apt-get install vpnc-scripts
   ```

2. **Find the script location** and make sure it's executable. For example:
   ```bash
   sudo chmod u+x /etc/vpnc/vpnc-script
   ```

3. **If OpenConnect still can't find it**, specify the script path explicitly when connecting:
   ```bash
   openconnect --script /etc/vpnc/vpnc-script https://vpn.rc.fas.harvard.edu/
   ```
   (Adjust the path to match where the script actually lives on your system.)

This is documented in the FASRC guide for connecting to the VPN from Linux [Connecting to the FAS RC VPN from Linux clients](https://docs.rc.fas.harvard.edu/kb/linux-vpn/).

question_88.question: I hit Ctrl-C on my srun job to stop it and it just printed some status about the tasks and kept running. How do I actually make it stop?
question_88.reference_answer: That is by design: a single <control-c> is an escape sequence that reports the state of all tasks associated with the srun command. To kill the job, press <control-c> twice within one second — that sends SIGINT to all tasks and starts a termination sequence of SIGCONT, SIGTERM and SIGKILL to all spawned tasks. A third <control-c> terminates srun itself immediately, without waiting for the remote tasks to exit or their I/O to complete. (Signal forwarding does not work at all for asynchronous steps launched with --async; use scancel --signal for those.)
question_88.answer:
This is a known behavior with `srun`. When you press `Ctrl-C`, `srun` prints a status message but **does not automatically kill the tasks** it launched. The tasks continue running in the background.

To actually stop the job, you need to explicitly send a termination signal to the job step. Here are your options:

1. **Use `scancel` on the job step ID**: If you know the job step ID (e.g., `12345.0`), run:
   ```bash
   scancel 12345.0
   ```
   If you're inside an interactive `srun` session, you can often use `scancel` with the job ID of the allocation.

2. **Send a signal to the srun process itself**: In some configurations, sending a stronger signal (like `SIGKILL`) to the `srun` process will also terminate the tasks. You can find the PID of the `srun` process and kill it:
   ```bash
   kill -9 <srun_pid>
   ```

3. **Use `--kill-on-bad-exit` or `--signal` options**: When launching `srun`, you can specify how it handles signals. For example, using `--signal=B:TERM` can help ensure tasks are terminated when `srun` receives a signal.

The key takeaway is that `Ctrl-C` on `srun` is **not** a reliable way to stop running tasks. You need to explicitly cancel the job step using `scancel` or kill the tasks directly.

For more details, see the [Slurm FAQ on srun termination behavior](https://slurm.schedmd.com/faq.html).
